# What a Digital Elevation Model Is, and Where I Am Guessing

A digital elevation model is a grid of heights. Each cell holds one number: how high the ground is, above some reference level, at the middle of that cell. That is nearly all of it. No rocks, no trees as objects, no roads. Just a sheet of numbers laid over a place.

What I understood: the grid is a sample, not the land. Cell size sets how much detail survives. Ten metres across and a ridge two metres wide is gone. The model is smooth where the real thing is jagged, and it has no idea what it left out.

Where I am guessing: I am not sure whether the height in a cell is the surface or the bare ground. Some models are made from laser returns that hit canopy and roofs, others from models that strip them off. I do not know which kind I was looking at, and the two give different maps of the same hill.

I also guess at the vertical error. A model can be off by a metre or more, and the error is not even. Flat ground is usually more trustworthy than steep ground, but I have not checked that against a survey, only against what I read.

So: a grid of heights, coarse, sampled, of uncertain surface type, with errors I cannot see from inside it. That is my understanding. Next time I should look for the metadata first and find out what the numbers are standing on.
